title: Tullio Phenomenon -- Introduction
content: The Tullio phenomenon is a symptom and physical examination finding characterized by sound-induced nystagmus or vertigo. Professor Pietro Tullio in Bologna, Italy, first described the phenomenon after experimental studies on pigeons in 1929. In humans, the phenomenon was first observed in patients with advanced syphilis, in whom labyrinthine fistulas produced a "mobile third window" in the inner ear. Subsequent reports and studies have demonstrated the Tullio phenomenon across multiple pathologies, including in individuals without identifiable inner-ear disease. [1] Currently, the phenomenon is most frequently associated with superior semicircular canal dehiscence (SCD). [2] [3] This activity emphasizes the relationship between the Tullio phenomenon and SCD, with brief consideration of other relevant pathologies.

title: Tullio Phenomenon -- Function
content: Professor Tullio served as director of the Laboratory of Experimental Physiology in Bologna during the early 20th century. His work was inspired by French physiologist Jean Flourens, who had observed that pigeons exhibited sudden, impulsive movements in the plane of a damaged semicircular canal. The majority of Tullio’s experiments were conducted on live pigeons. These birds provided a favorable model for studying labyrinthine physiology due to their anatomical characteristics and prominent head nystagmus, which permitted direct observation of vestibular responses. [4]

title: Tullio Phenomenon -- Function
content: Initial experiments involved observing the movement of water on tuning forks, followed by observing particle currents in vibrating water. Subsequent studies introduced particles into the endolymph and perilymph of pigeons and observed resulting current movements in response to sound. These currents produced rhythmic waves against the ampulla, generating head movements in the plane of the corresponding canal. Increasing sound intensity caused the currents to oscillate, inducing nystagmus in the animal at a frequency corresponding to current oscillation.

title: Tullio Phenomenon -- Function
content: Sound stimulation affected all 3 semicircular canals simultaneously. However, differences in current intensity among the canals determined the direction and magnitude of head movement. Opening a semicircular canal allowed its current to dominate the other 2 canals, resulting in observable movement of the open canal.

title: Tullio Phenomenon -- Function
content: Tullio subsequently analyzed pigeons’ head movements following the opening of each semicircular canal by attaching a lever to the beak, producing a graphic record of reflexes elicited by sound stimuli. Head movements occurred in the plane of the opened canal. Application of cocaine to the osseous openings paralyzed the nerve endings, preventing further head movement in response to stimulation.

title: Tullio Phenomenon -- Function
content: Opening all 3 canals resulted in immobility of the heads because the fenestrations neutralized one another. Head rotation about an anteroposterior axis could be induced, with the rotation directed toward the unaffected ear, reflecting utricular excitation that persisted after the ampullae of all 3 canals had been paralyzed. Later experiments replicated lesions induced by Flourens and demonstrated that irritative stretching of ampullae nerves produces labyrinthine ataxia, a condition now termed "Flourens syndrome."

title: Tullio Phenomenon -- Function
content: After approximately 20 years of research, Tullio published findings in the 1929 work Some Experiments and Considerations on Experimental Otology and Phonetics. The study was nominated for the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1932. Subsequent investigators reported the Tullio phenomenon in additional conditions, highlighting its relevance to labyrinthine fistula. Initially, the phenomenon in humans was considered indicative of congenital syphilis, in which patients developed labyrinthine osteomyelitis. Miliary gumma within the endosteum, thought to signal congenital syphilis, could produce labyrinthine fistulas. These fistulas were believed to underlie the Tullio phenomenon. Cawthorne proposed that the phenomenon occurred in humans only when more than 1 mobile window opened into the inner ear on the vestibular side of the vestibular membrane. [5] Studies conducted over the past 60 years provided results demonstrating that the Tullio phenomenon occurs across a wide range of clinical and experimental contexts.

title: Tullio Phenomenon -- Function
content: Kacker and Hinchcliffe reported a positive Tullio sign in 2 patients with Meniere syndrome who had negative fistula tests, as well as in a patient with a history of trauma, in whom the stapes had subsumed into the vestibule. [6] Serologic testing for syphilis was negative in all 3 cases. [7] Kwee investigated the incidence of the Tullio phenomenon in a cohort of 150 deaf children and identified 50 participants with a positive Tullio phenomenon in 1 or both ears, representing 76 of 300 ears. Nystagmus consistently occurred toward the stimulated ear. Additional manifestations were observed in some instances, including deviation of the head away from the source of the tone and subjective sensations of dizziness. No occurrence of the Tullio phenomenon was noted in the absence of a calorically excitable labyrinth. [8]

title: Tullio Phenomenon -- Function
content: Nadol described a patient with bilateral deafness following an upper respiratory infection in childhood, a positive Hennebert sign, and fibrous adhesions within the membranous labyrinth (vestibulofibrosis), suggesting a pathological basis for a positive fistula sign despite an intact tympanic membrane. [9] Subsequent studies' results reported similar histologic findings in various postinflammatory or progressive inner ear disorders, including congenital syphilis, viral labyrinthitis, and Meniere disease. These observations may represent the pathophysiologic mechanism underlying sound-induced vestibular symptoms in patients with endolymphatic hydrops. Distension of the membranous labyrinth may permit contact with the medial aspect of the stapes footplate. In the Erlich study, all patients with Meniere disease exhibited a positive Tullio phenomenon. [10]

title: Tullio Phenomenon -- Function
content: The high incidence of the Tullio phenomenon in healthy subjects and patients with diverse cochleovestibular disorders indicates that sound-induced vestibular stimulation may be elicited under appropriate monitoring. Parker investigated the physiologic response of the vestibular system to acoustic stimulation and demonstrated that pressure changes or high-intensity sound produced measurable stapes displacement, corresponding changes in perilymph pressure, and alterations in vestibular neuron firing rates. Normal individuals exhibited vestibular symptoms, such as nystagmus, in response to intense pressure or audio-frequency stimulation. Management of the Tullio phenomenon depends on the underlying etiology. [11]

title: Tullio Phenomenon -- Issues of Concern
content: Although the Tullio phenomenon cannot serve as a diagnostic tool for a specific disease, as initially hypothesized by Tullio, it may indicate cochleovestibular or other otologic pathology warranting further investigation. A detailed history and thorough physical examination can narrow the differential diagnosis. Additional testing may be necessary, including audiometry, tympanometry, stapedial reflex testing, fistula testing, videonystagmography, electrocochleography, brain magnetic resonance imaging, and computed tomography. Patients frequently exhibit ‘‘supernormal’’ bone-conduction audiometric thresholds ipsilateral to the lesion and reduced vestibular-evoked myogenic potential thresholds. [12]

title: Tullio Phenomenon -- Issues of Concern
content: The Tullio phenomenon should be differentiated from Minor syndrome, characterized by dehiscence of the superior semicircular canal. Most patients with the Tullio phenomenon have SCD. A variant of the phenomenon has been reported in patients with idiopathic bilateral vestibular failure, who present with horizontal rather than torsional eye movements in response to sound and pressure. [13]

title: Tullio Phenomenon -- Clinical Significance
content: The Tullio phenomenon is most commonly associated with SCD syndrome (SCDS). [14] Additional conditions linked with the phenomenon include the following: Otosclerosis Congenital syphilis Ménière disease Idiopathic intracranial hypertension [15] Perilymph fistula Cholesteatoma with semicircular canal erosion and fenestration Head trauma Normal individuals Post stapedectomy Post tympanomastoidectomy Collapsed canal syndrome Congenital deafness Seronegative Lyme borreliosis Middle ear osteoma [16] [17] [18] [19] [20]

title: Tullio Phenomenon -- Clinical Significance
content: SCDS was first described in 1998 and is characterized by sound-induced vertigo and eye movements, chronic dysequilibrium, conductive hearing loss, and decreased bone-conduction thresholds at lower frequencies. Conductive hyperacusis may produce autophony, pulsatile tinnitus, or perception of eye movements, the latter termed "oscillopsia." [21] [22] The disorder results from the absence of bone over the superior semicircular canal.

title: Tullio Phenomenon -- Clinical Significance
content: The pathogenesis of SCDS remains debated, with evidence supporting both congenital and acquired factors. Congenital thinning of the lateral skull base and the otic capsule overlying the superior semicircular canal is considered necessary but not sufficient for syndrome manifestation. This conclusion follows from the observation that the radiographic prevalence of thin bone exceeds the clinical prevalence of SCDS.

title: Tullio Phenomenon -- Clinical Significance
content: The leading explanatory model is the 2-hit theory, which posits that individuals with preexisting thinner bone overlying the superior semicircular canal are more vulnerable. Symptomatic presentation occurs after a secondary event, such as head trauma, forceful Valsalva maneuver, or exposure to loud noise, which causes the thin bone to fracture, creating a functional dehiscence. This 3rd window then triggers the characteristic vestibular and auditory symptoms. [23] Mixed vertical-torsional nystagmus develops when patients with SCDS exhibit the Tullio phenomenon, with the slow phase rotating upward and away from the affected ear. This nystagmus is aligned with the plane of the affected superior semicircular canal and is pathognomonic of SCDS. [24]

title: Tullio Phenomenon -- Clinical Significance
content: The superior canal may be either excited or inhibited, depending on the type of stimulus. Excitation occurs from ampullofugal displacement of the cupula due to positive external auditory canal (EAC) pressure generated by tragal compression, sound, or nasal Valsalva. Inhibition occurs from ampullopetal deflection of the cupula caused by negative EAC pressure from jugulovenous compression or glottis Valsalva. The Hennebert sign may also be present, in which nystagmus is induced by pressure in the EAC. [25]

title: Tullio Phenomenon -- Clinical Significance
content: Diagnosis of SCDS relies on computed tomography (CT) imaging of the temporal bone, which demonstrates thinning or dehiscence of the bone overlying the superior semicircular canal. Required CT imaging includes the Pöschl and Stenver views, described as a "sagittal oblique projection perpendicular to the superior semicircular canal loop" and an "oblique coronal reconstruction parallel to the petrous portion of the temporal bone," respectively. These specialized planes improve detection by aligning the imaging plane with the canal, facilitating clearer identification of the missing bone. [26] Recent studies indicate that MRI can achieve diagnostic precision comparable to CT. However, CT is the most commonly employed modality. [27]

title: Tullio Phenomenon -- Clinical Significance
content: Surgical intervention is the mainstay of treatment for SCDS because it is effective, safe, and associated with a low complication rate. Canal plugging involves the placement of bone chips and fascia, followed by coverage with bone cement via a middle fossa approach. Results from recent studies demonstrate that the transmastoid approach reduces operative time and hospital stay while providing audiometric and clinical outcomes comparable to the middle fossa approach. [28] Other surgical techniques include endoscopic, transcranial, or endaural approaches. [29] Minimally invasive methods, such as round window reinforcement, have also been explored. [30] [31] In cases with mild-to-moderate symptoms, medical management with diuretics, such as acetazolamide, has shown promising results in symptom control. [32]

title: Tullio Phenomenon -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: Although the Tullio phenomenon is infrequently observed in clinical practice, healthcare professionals in specialties such as family and internal medicine must recognize its significance. Referral to appropriate specialists is indicated for further evaluation or management. Clinicians performing visual, auditory, or neurological assessments should be familiar with this sign.

title: Tullio Phenomenon -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: Treatment of individuals with the Tullio phenomenon requires an interprofessional approach to ensure patient-centered care and optimize outcomes. Evidence-based strategies should guide the development of treatment plans to maximize efficacy and minimize adverse effects. Application of principles, including technical skill, strategic planning, ethical practice, communication, and care coordination, enhances patient-centered care, improving both clinical outcomes and team performance in the management of the Tullio phenomenon.
